excerpt: During development, scans run automatically as part of CI/CD pipelines when code is committed or merge requests are created.
Security findings appear directly in merge requests and IDEs, notifying developers before code is merged.
Outside the development cycle, you can run security scans on demand, or schedule them to run at regular intervals.
Application security testing scans your project’s source code, dependencies, libraries, and container images.
Enable SAST in your project by using either the UI or editing your project’s GitLab CI/CD configuration file.
SAST scans happen automatically with each commit, giving you immediate feedback without disrupting your workflow.
For Ultimate tier customers with a GitLab Duo add-on, false positive detection runs automatically after each security scan and provides confidence scores with explanations for each assessment.
This agentic approach uses multi-shot reasoning to resolve vulnerabilities with minimal human intervention.
Selecting the file path opens the corresponding line in the code view.
Merge request changes view: Shows inline annotations for changed lines.
In Ultimate, you can also download the security scan results:
The push is blocked if secrets are detected, unless you skip secret push protection.
When a secret is detected you can choose to edit the input and remove the secret or, if it’s a false positive, save the description or comment.
For some secret types, GitLab can even automatically revoke the exposed secret.
If a secret is committed to a repository, GitLab records the exposure in the vulnerability report.
Dependency scanning identifies known security vulnerabilities in your project’s dependencies, including runtime, development, and transitive (nested) packages.
Catching newly disclosed vulnerabilities without re-running pipelines
When a merge request that bumps a dependency has a failed pipeline, GitLab Duo can analyze the failure and provide fixes to resolve it.
An experiment that analyzes the runtime behavior of your dependencies to surface suspicious or malicious activity beyond known vulnerabilities.
Teams orchestrate, agents execute, turning issues into merge requests, remediating vulnerabilities, and reviewing code, all inside the guardrails you set.
Planning, source control, and CI/CD in one platform.
Every agent action shows up in the audit trail.
Connect any MCP-compatible agent to GitLab, keep secrets under your existing permissions, and get every merge request to the right reviewer, faster.
Pick the right model for each job.

After moving from self-hosted git to GitLab, a user found the CI, namespacing and issue tracking 'truly great and well thought of'. But performance was 'abysmal': whole days with no deploys because CI workers didn't run (even self-hosted ones), and pushes taking minutes versus seconds on GitHub.
One user loves GitLab and uses a private instance at work, but won't host public projects on it for one reason: you can't hide your email address shown in commits.

A user said migrating repos is straightforward with the GitHub importer. It brings over repo data, issues, pull requests, wikis, milestones, labels, release notes, and review comments, and keeps private/public visibility.
Several users hit 502 errors on GitLab.com during the import spike after the Microsoft/GitHub news. One noted that Bitbucket was up while GitLab was crashing.
A user wants to move to GitLab, but their username has been held for over two years by someone with an empty group. With no way to contact them to ask for the name, they remain on GitHub.

A user values that GitLab is open source at its core, so anyone can run their own instance or fork it if the company moves in a direction the community dislikes. Another has long run GitLab in a VM via a TurnKey Linux appliance.

During the 2017 database incident, a quoted line from GitLab's live report was widely cited: 'out of 5 backup/replication techniques deployed none are working reliably or set up in the first place.' Commenters noted the S3 backup bucket was empty and pg_dump had been failing silently.

A self-managed GitLab EE user said backups broke starting in 8.15 because a 'readable' date stamp was added to backup file names without proper testing. It was somewhat fixed, but they still saw issues in 8.16.
A user said they have loved the product for about two years. Many commenters praised GitLab's transparency in publishing the raw incident timeline, calling it 'amazingly transparent and honest.'
A commenter praised GitLab's openness but said the incident shows why you shouldn't trust a cloud service to keep your data safe. They run and test their own backups instead.
A user loves GitLab but still uses GitHub because many services offering free accounts to open source projects, such as TravisCI, don't integrate with GitLab.

A user switched their personal projects and three organizations from GitHub to GitLab over the past year. They were won over by GitLab's data centers in Asia and Europe, saying GitHub is extremely slow in Asia.
A commenter sees GitLab as competing more with Atlassian than with GitHub, noting Mattermost is bundled with GitLab.
